utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... we don't need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sarkanovic. I believe it was two days ago you had mentioned that when you -- following the interview with the detained person and following that person having dictated or saying aloud what was going to go into the statement, that it would be typed up, and then you also mentioned that you would append your own comments. Did you do that in every case? Do you remember whether you did it in this case of Mr. Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never added my comments in any of the cases. What the person stated in the interview when the statement was taken, that was the only thing that was entered into the record of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, you did say not that you put things into the statement but that following the statement, there might be a separate sheet where you put your comments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what you mean. That was done in the case of Dagovic. On the morning of the 17th of April, I saw him with weapons in his hands, together with the Atic brothers, with Fadil Sabanovic, I think there was Bicic brothers there as well. And after that, when I came to take the statement from him, when I was interviewing him - I don't know which day that was - I spoke to him, and he told me what he told me. But it was according to my own knowledge, based on what I saw on the 17th, in the morning, I wrote an official note, and this should have been attached either to the statement of Dagovic or added to the statement of any of the others who were with him in the group then it would have included my official note about what I had myself observed on the morning of the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now that we are talking about the statements in respect of the questions that the Prosecutor asked, first I would like to clarify one matter. You have already answered something in relation to this, but I'd like us to elaborate on this. Here you said during the cross-examination already that each person that you interviewed, after which you compiled a written statement, first of all, you would ask them whether this person wanted to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You've already answered that. Were there any persons who did not wish to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And these persons who gave their statements, can you tell me, if only just roughly: How many, approximately, percentage-wise, how many of them said: Yes, that's correct. I had weapons. I was a member of units that were established. Can you tell me based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's cross-examining. He's putting words in the witness's mouth. He's giving the answer to the witness: How many told you this precise thing? There's a proper way of asking the question, in my submission, but that's not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. He's asking him the number or the percentage of the persons who told him what the counsel has cited to the witness. He's asking for the number. He's not asking whether anybody told him this; he's asking for the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I must have heard something different to what's on the transcript. Maybe I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You may answer this question. How many of them refuted this? How many said that they did not have weapons?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately 90 per cent of them refused to say, that is, what they stated was that they did have weapons and that they were not members of paramilitary formations. And I have already answered this question when asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So 90 per cent of people that you interviewed said they had no connection with weapons or with units; is that correct? Is that true to say?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, since we come from the same legal system and based on a number of questions that the Prosecutor asked you, perhaps it would be a good idea to clarify: What happens to a statement that you take? You drew us a diagram here, and perhaps you could tell me: Considering that you told me that you passed the statements on to your superior, Milos Savic, can you tell me what happens to these statements afterwards? What's the further procedure? Who does what with these statements?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Savic would give these statements to the chief of the station, Todorovic, Stevan Todorovic. He would then assess whether, on the basis of the statement and any other evidence that was gathered whether there were elements of the criminal offence, and then there was -- this was reported to the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. So if the chief would say that there were -- there was ground to file charges, then he would then pass it on to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who signs the charges?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be done by the chief of the station, Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There were a number of objections during my cross-examination to speculation. Can we please clarify whether this is in fact what happened or what should have happened. The word -- my learned friend is using "would" in the subjunctive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought he was asking the witness what the procedure used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very simply, it is what I'm asking for: What is the procedure. And definitely I will ask him -- my colleague will not have a problem whether this is how it happened during war. And I will have no problem about asking the witness this. I just want now to establish what is the procedure of how does these statements -- are used in further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I'm just clarifying. The questions were -- seem to relate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can you just sit down, please. Mr. Lazarevic, can you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, so when the prosecutor physically receives the charges and the statement, what does he do then?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this report on the charges and any other documents that are attached to the charges, then he assesses whether he can raise an indictment, issue an indictment. He then proposes that an investigation should be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just stop here now. So we have two ways that the prosecutor can choose: Either he can go with the indictment --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With direct indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But of course he can also reject it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And another way would be for the criminal charges to then be forwarded to the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another possibility further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not objecting. I don't know when they are talking about. Before Mr. Lazarevic asked what happens, the witness answered - this was my clarification earlier - Todorovic would. Now it seems to be talking about the general procedure, and I'm not sure whether it was before when he was a police inspector or during the two months when he was employed -- when he was working during the war. That is very important. I just ask for clarification as to when he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I can answer that by posing certain questions to the witness, and I believe it will be -- we are strictly talking about the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When? When? Before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Pose two questions. Just wait one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Prosecutor asked you under which law, in terms of procedure, was applied.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law on criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is what we talked about the time before the war. Now we're talking about the breaking out of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Republika Srpska, and the Federation, as they are called now, what is the law that was applied in terms of criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same law. The same law. This is the law that was inherited from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was the same law applied in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So now we can draw the conclusion, from what you've said, that before the war and throughout the war, there was one and the same law that was applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was in force before the war and throughout the war, in the entire territory of BH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now speaking about the situation which is regulated by this Law on Criminal Procedure, and we have come to the investigating judge. What does an investigating judge do when he receives, according to law? What does he do when he receives a statement, a statement of a person given to a police organ, according to the then valid regulations?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again, can we clarify when? Are we talking about the period when the witness worked in the police station, April, May, and June and if so, was that the procedure that was actually followed? Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness has said that during the war they followed the same type of law. They inherited the same law from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Procedure is a different thing to law, Your Honour, and that's what I'm trying to work out, whether they are talking about the procedure that was followed April, May, June, when the witness was working there or the law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But from the answers of the witness and the questions of the counsel, it's the same thing. It's the procedure they are discussing. Who did what, where did the statements do -- where were the statements taken. Mr. Lazarevic, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So investigating judge would then receive a statement that was taken in the police. What would he do with the statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would then take it out of the case, place it in an envelope, and would seal it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This statement, according to the rules that were valid then, the laws that were applying then, valid in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina before and throughout the entire war, could this statement have been used during the criminal proceedings against the person who had given the statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: What was the only condition according to which this statement could have been used?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the accused wished this statement to be used himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that we have now sorted out the importance of the statements given in the police station. But now, so that the Prosecutor can have the full picture of all this: What's your experience, and do you know about this, whether this procedure, during the war, was this respected during the war? Did Stevan Todorovic file charges according to rules, et cetera? If you know.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So following on from that point: Do you know whether, in fact, an investigating judge or judges became involved in any of the cases where you had taken and witnessed the statements of detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether that would happen. In fact, the judges are included according to the wishes of the prosecutor, if there is need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are still dealing with the then valid regulations, and we have three stages of criminal proceedings. First -- go on. You say them so that I don't lead you. Can you tell me: What are the three stages, according to the then valid regulations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be pre-criminal proceedings, done by the police; then the indictment, done by the prosecutor; and the trial, which is conducted by the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us start with the pre-criminal proceedings. This is to do -- this is something that you did. This is to do with the organs of the police. First of all, was it obligatory to remand a person in custody for everyone who would be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Specifically now, during your work at the police station during the war, which is part of April, May, June, were there persons who gave statements and who, after that, were released and were not detained?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. There were. There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think from the question of Judge Williams, there were -- it was obvious that certain persons were released.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I said that that was Dzevad Jusufovic and Sabanovic. Except that I'd like to add Safet Hadzialijagic, also known as Pop and Hasan Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In relation -- sorry. Did you want to add something? In relation to this, I wanted to ask you another thing: Who made a decision that these people should be released and not kept in custody in detention?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lazarevic. Just for the sake of clarity: Mr. Sarkanovic, did you mention, I think before the break today, that Mr. Fadil Sabanovic -- you had seen him with the Bicic brothers, I think? Is this the same person that you had seen earlier on in the -- on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same person. The same person. They were very near my apartment, and it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And did you mention whether or not he had a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned that he had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So you saw him, he had weapons, he was interviewed, and then he was released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I need to ask for one clarification in the transcript. It's on page 54, line 25. And the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lazarevic please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, if you put your microphone near you. Can you repeat what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a clarification on page 55, line 25. Instead of asked Safet Hadzialijagic, I'd like to add Safet Hadzialijagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So, sir, obviously there were cases of persons being released, for whom there was clear evidence to the effect that they had weapons and that they were in some kind of organised unit. According to your testimony, there were also situations in which people against whom no evidence was possessed were nevertheless held in custody.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who decided on who would be released and who would not be released?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you a certain number of questions concerning the possible reasons that Mr. Zaric had to ask for Mr. Tihic to be set free. He suggested to you that a possible reason could have been that these lists had been forged and that perhaps Mr. Zaric knew that. So let's deal with that reason first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. I didn't say that. I said it gave you reasons to cast doubts on the authenticity of the document, at least insofar as it concerned Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which is not the same as forging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Reason to cast doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I apologise. I really didn't want to mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, one of the reasons was doubts regarding the authenticity of these documents. Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your last answer, whether you remember that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember the answer too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is evidence before this Trial Chamber, or rather, a statement of a man who had personally compiled these lists, or rather, the list of self-organised citizens, and confirmed its authenticity? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't want us to go into speculation. Furthermore, another possible reason that the Prosecutor mentioned as a reason that could have led Mr. Zaric to ask for Mr. Tihic to be set free was that Mr. Zaric was convinced that he was innocent. Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you the following question: Could a possible reason could have been their personal relationships, the years-long friendship between Mr. Tihic and Mr. Zaric? Could that have been a reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. It's cross-examining the witness. It's putting words in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think he should have asked whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Whether the witness knew of any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I'm going to ask you something that has to do with your very own assessment regarding Mr. Tihic and his release. Mr. Tihic was, no doubt, president of the SDA in Bosanski Samac; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What do you think? So I'm interested in your opinion. What do you think: Would the release of Mr. Tihic contribute to calming the situation in town?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is now asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's also cross-examination, putting words into the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to ask you some other questions, then, related to the release of a certain number of persons from detention. Did you personally know or did you see this perhaps, when it had to do with some other persons for whom Mr. Zaric also made an effort in order to have them released? So not only Tihic, the man we had already been discussing.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said - I don't know whether I said it yesterday or the day before yesterday - that I was present on one occasion when Mr. Zaric asked Mr. Todorovic to have some persons released, and he flatly refused that. And then, let me say this once again, that I said to Mr. Zaric that it would be better for him to ask for something else so that he could get what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So the request for Mr. Tihic to be released was not the only one of its kind that Mr. Zaric addressed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Milos Savic, yourself and Mr. Zaric, to the extent to which he was there, what was your position vis-a-vis the detention of these people, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, it was negative. Notably, the fact that they were kept in custody, because we thought that if there were no grounds for detention, then people should be allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, I'm just going to ask you some questions related to Mr. Dagovic. You heard the exchange between Their Honours and me about this. You've already -- we've already extensively covered the situation of the prisoners in custody, and I'm not going to go back over that. Mr. Dagovic was arrested on the 5th of May, 1992. While in custody, he was severely and repeatedly beaten by the people who were detaining him. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I talked to Mr. Dagovic, but, as I recall this, he was always dressed up, he always looked well. I think that on that occasion, there were no visible signs of beatings or anything like that on him. Perhaps it was later. I know him well. He was a neighbour of mine. I'm sure that it would have been noticeable on him in respect of the way in which he dressed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you know that if a person is beaten, they're not necessarily beaten about the face in a way which is immediately visible to someone else? You will accept that a person can be beaten on the back, stomach, legs, genitals, without any marks showing on their face? You'll accept that, won't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that he had not been beaten. I said that there were no noticeable, visible signs of beating on him. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, there's evidence before this Trial Chamber that Mr. Dagovic was severely and repeatedly beaten in custody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the witness's answer is clear. The witness is not denying that this -- Mr. Esad Dagovic was beaten. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic -- I'm sorry. The only way I can put my question, Your Honour, is to premise it on that and then move to the question. If the witness is accepting, you accept that Mr. Dagovic was severely and repeatedly beaten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you're going to repeat that, I'll order you to sit down, because we can't go on discussing one point. This witness has clearly said that he's not denying that this particular witness was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm talking about before interrogation, Your Honour not in the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How would he know?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only moving to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because he explained that when he saw him, he didn't have visible marks, so it follows that you didn't know whether on the hidden parts he was beaten before or after interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, if you can accept that although you didn't see marks, he had been severely and repeatedly beaten before interrogation, you would accept that he would not have been in a psychological or physically fit state to undergo interrogation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you accept that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are statements before the -- two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic specifically asked about the circumstances of what was in those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking, based upon the evidence before the Trial Chamber of Mr. Dagovic, to accept something and to move to the point as to the circumstances of the taking -- Mr. Dagovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Just ask him what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought that I was by putting it that way. I thought I was getting him to accept a premise for which my next question would be that. To get to that point, I was asking him to accept that a person in those circumstances would not be psychologically or physically fit for interrogation, then move to the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A person who has been severely and repeatedly beaten before interrogation would not be psychologically or physically fit for interrogation in the police cells; you accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that's right, but it doesn't really have to be that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Sarkanovic, whether you can remember whether you or Mr. Savic, when you were together interviewing Mr. Dagovic, whether either you or he ever said to Mr. Dagovic, perhaps other detainees as well, did you ever ask whether he had been beaten, whether he was fit to answer questions? Was there ever any conversation as to that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every detained citizen that I talked to, after this person would be brought into my office, before starting the official interview, we would always chat. We would exchange a few sentences about general matters. I asked everyone whether they wanted to give a statement. On some of them, there were traces of beatings; on some more, on some less. I've already said that. Although there were some on which there were no visible traces. Not a single one of them looked to me as if he could not make a statement. In my opinion, Dragan Lukac and Grga Zubak were beaten most of all. He did not look to me as if he could not make a statement. He even dictated it into the record himself, Dragan Lukac did. I did not speak to Grga, though, but I heard that he had been beaten, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just would like you to answer the question that I asked, which is whether you actually said to any of these persons you were interviewing, whether you actually asked them: Have you been beaten? Where did you get those bruises on your face? Or what have you. Did you ever try to find out why and what had been done to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask, simply because I saw some of these beatings myself through the window, because the TO is in front of my window. And it was known that there was no one else who could have been beating them but the specials, or policemen, if there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, there's evidence before this Court that you and Mr. Savic did not use force, but immediately before Mr. Dagovic gave his statements, and immediately after, he would usually be beaten and would have to give a subsequent statement, and that the statement, not implicating you, was not deemed satisfactory, he would be beaten again and would be expected to provide another statement. You would accept, in those circumstances, because you didn't see -- you didn't see these beatings of him, that any statement that he gave to you or Mr. Savic would have to be unreliable, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: Had Dragan Lukac said that, or Grga Zubak, I would have agreed completely. But Dagovic - I repeat this once again - I did not notice any signs of beating on him. I mean, I don't agree with that, at least in this specific case. I mean, had Dragan Lukac said that, or somebody else who had been beaten a bit more or way too much, then I would have agreed. But in view of the condition that he was in when I saw him, no, I can't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't wish to take it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sarkanovic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. We are finished now. You may go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much as well for this correct treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe before we bring our other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it is a good time to tender three more 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are those the last ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the last three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For your...?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From our list of 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we have them? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The first statement that we would like to tender into evidence is a statement of Mato Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number for this one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be treated as document D45/4 ID and D45/4 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The next statement we would like to tender into evidence is the statement of Jasenica Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be treated as document D46/4 ter ID and D46/4 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the last one is the statement of Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be treated as document D47/4 ter ID and D47/4 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe it's a good moment to ask the -- we still don't have any response from the Prosecution as a draft statement of Nizam Ramusovic that we are discussing with the Prosecution whether they have intention to cross-examine this witness or at least to give us their position in respect to that witness, so we can organise certification of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution? The legal officer was -- did ask the Prosecution to deal with this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. It seems that we have overlooked that. Could we have until tomorrow to do so, and maybe address the Court orally tomorrow or file something by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So you deal with it first thing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's orally, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Orally or filing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Orally. Yes. Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And before we bring in the next witness, Mr. Pisarevic would like to address the Court. It is in respect to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have rather a new, fresh situation regarding the witness that we have to call, who is waiting to testify. He has asked me to request Your Honours if he would be able to testify in closed session today, because this is a request, in fact, that comes from his family, of many members, these family members are strewn all over Western Europe, working there. He doesn't have, himself, his own personal reasons that he should be a witness testifying in closed session, but he would wish to respect the worries and the anxieties of his brothers, sisters, and his family, and to protect him in some way from some possible consequences, because he is coming to testify here before this Honourable Court. Now, this is what we are requesting: That the next witness to be called testifies in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the basis of their anxiety?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the basis is that their brothers and sisters, and many relatives, are working temporarily in Western Europe, in many different countries. And because in Western Europe there is a large number of other ethnicities and possibly also victims, while he's here coming to testify as a Defence witness, he has been asked by his relatives that when he comes to testify, that he testifies in closed session, because they have some indications, some possible signs that this would make it much more difficult for them where they are, it could make it more difficult for their status in those countries, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Has this got to do with his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, we oppose the application. I was informed recently - I can't remember precisely when - by Mr. Lazarevic that in fact the concern of the witness related to a daughter who is living in a European country. It may be that the concern is more -- is larger and wider than that, but I was informed that it was related to the concerns of a daughter living in a European country. The concerns have not been articulated or expanded upon so that you can assess just how serious or valid or realistic those concerns are. You've simply been told that they're worried and concerned. If the relatives are living outside of Bosanski Samac, in other countries in Europe, then one would have thought that their concerns would be considerably less than people living in the area. So at this stage, the Prosecution's submission is they haven't even made it to first base, so to speak, in terms of raising anything that you can reliably look at in order to assess whether or not the evidence would be -- needs to be in closed session. All that we know is concerns of family members. Well, that simply is not enough. The prima facie principle is public justice, and in my submission, you should ensure that this witness's testimony is in open session. Furthermore, it's been, I think, extremely well known that this witness is going to testify. His position in Bosanski Samac would be clear to all observers of this trial or interested observers of this trial, and the content of his testimony, again, is something that -- the general content of his testimony is again something that should be well known to all interested observers of this trial. So in my submission, there's nothing realistic that's been raised by the Defence calling for closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Having considered the submissions of the parties, the Trial Chamber is not satisfied that there are -- there is a reasonable basis for this request that the evidence of the witness should be given in closed session, especially that the witness himself has no concerns at all. So the witness will give evidence in open session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Pisarevic, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Antic. Before you introduce yourself to the Honourable Judges, I will inform you of the fact that we have made a submission to the Trial Chamber in respect of the protective measures that we have discussed; however, the decision of the Trial Chamber is that these reasons that have been raised are not justified enough in order for the protective measures to be approved. I have to tell you this before you start to testify so that you know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Since we are speaking the same language, I will ask you to pause before you answer my question. Please answer slowly and articulately so that the interpreters can interpret. However, if there is a problem, if you cannot hear the sound or picture on the screen, so that we can all have communication, those of us who are in this courtroom, please let us know in some way so that we can resolve these problems. Now, please, could you tell me - that is, could you tell the Chamber - your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: My name is Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: 6th of March, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you were born?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Batkusa, municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me which republic that is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: That is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your ancestors, do they also come from that place, Batkusa, and how long has your ancestral family lived there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are from Batkusa. The origin of my family, that is, the length of how long my family has lived there, is about a hundred years, just over a hundred years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete primary school?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Four years of primary school I completed in the village of Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you complete secondary school?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I completed four years of primary school in the village of Obudovac, I continued the lower years of grammar school, the junior schools, in Bosanski Samac, and I completed that in 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you -- what school did you enroll into after the grammar school?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: In 1956, after completing the grammar school, I enrolled in the secondary agricultural school in Bijeljina, which I completed in 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you continue your education? And if you did, where?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I completed my secondary agricultural school and worked for about a year, I then went to serve my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell me: Where did you serve? The JNA? And when?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA in 1961 and 1962, in the school for reserve officers in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you completed this reserve officers' school in Bileca, what was your rank when you left, when you left that school?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I completed the school, I was sent to work in the JNA, in another unit, as a work practice and after I finished that, my rank was second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your life and your career, did you do any military exercises? Did you continue to advance in your rank? And in fact, what interests me is: What was your rank in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I left the JNA, with the rank of second lieutenant in reserve, because of completing the establishment rank force with the reserve officers, I was not appointed to a unit, assigned to any unit, but after the Territorial Defence was established in 1968, I was then assigned to the Territorial Defence as the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long were you there in the Territorial Defence, and how did your career then proceed, and what were the functions that you did?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I entered the Territorial Defence, I was sent to many different exercises, manoeuvres, for professional development and after I spent a certain number of years in the Territorial Defence, I would then be given according ranks. First of all, there would be lieutenant; and then after several successful years at the Territorial Defence, I would then be promoted to the rank of captain; and then after another number of years and many successful exercises, I would be promoted to the rank of the Captain First Class. And so in 1991, that is the rank that I held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: After you completed your serving in the JNA, what other schools did you complete?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I completed my military service in 1962, I enrolled in the higher teacher training college in Sarajevo, which I completed successfully in 1964, and so I was qualified to work as a teacher of physics and chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you continue your professional development, your studies and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After I completed this higher teacher training college, I worked at the primary school as a teacher; and then, in 1973, I then left the school and went to work as an administrative clerk at the authorities of the Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you complete -- do you have a university degree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1967 [as interpreted] I enrolled as part time in Belgrade, the faculty of National Defence, and I obtained my degree into two years, that is, I got my degree in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... transcript on page 73, line 6. The witness actually said: "In 1977."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Instead of "1977," it's "1979."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we just have the year again from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He listed in 1977 and completed in 1979. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which year did you enroll?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I started the National Defence university at 1977 and I got my degree in 1979. So that was in two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you worked as a teacher most of your career, if I understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you just please list the schools that you worked in.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I worked only at the primary school, Mitra Trifunovic Bosanski Samac and at the secondary school centre as a teacher in the secondary school in Bosanski Samac secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: During your work, did you have any public posts that you were not linked to education?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: During my career, I was at a public position from 1969 to 1973. I was -- as a volunteer. I was a vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Samac. And from 1977 -- from 1987 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: -- until 1991 [Realtime transcript read in error "1981], I was the chief of the secretariat of the interior in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were a chief of the secretariat of the interior until 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So there's been a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Until the 1st of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your status now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Now I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me: Where do you live now? You don't have to give your address; just the town, municipality.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I now live in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, throughout your life, you've lived in Bosanski Samac, that is, in Batkusa and Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Batkusa, and from 1964 to date, I have been living in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned this Territorial Defence staff that you were a member of, you are a Serb by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At this Territorial Defence staff of the Bosanski Samac municipality, were there officers, reserve military officers, of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Throughout the period from 1968 that this Territorial Defence staff operated, always in its structure there were members of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: Were you a member of the League of Communists; and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Communists until 1987, when I started to work at the organ of the interior, and because of the employment within this organ, I then could not be a member of a party organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So as a policeman, you were not allowed to be politicised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you now a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. From recently, I am a member of PDP Mladen Ivanic's party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us talk about the time before the breakout of hostilities in the municipality of Samac, that is, before the beginning of 1992 and the end of the 1991. Do you recall that in the municipality of Samac and in the town of Samac, certain activities were undertaken by the Yugoslav People's Army with respect to establishment of units of the Yugoslav People's Army? Can you tell us what you can recall.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the latter part of 1991, secretariat National Defence called two meetings, and two meetings were held, of all reserve officers who at that time lived in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you just wait a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it is time for a break now. Could we have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have our break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before this break, you said that there were two meetings. Can you give us a bit more detail about these meetings? Who spoke at the meetings? Who was present? And what was said at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Practically all the officers that lived in Samac then responded to the invitation to attend the first meeting. At this meeting, the situation, the political situation in Yugoslavia, was discussed. The problems related to the functioning of the Yugoslav People's Army. As for the second meeting, far less people came, because of the well-known positions of the national parties regarding the calls that were being made that they should leave the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, at the first meeting, all the officers were there, regardless of their ethnic background: Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and others; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Officers from the ranks of the Serb, Croat, and Muslim peoples attended the first meeting, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What are these well-known positions that you just referred to? What did you mean? Which positions? Of which leaders? Which ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: These were the positions of the leaderships of the national parties, namely, the HDZ and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who spoke at this meeting from amongst the active-duty officers of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: As for active-duty officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, Stevan Nikolic spoke and some of his co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Stevan Nikolic, did he hold a rank?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of the 17th Tactical Group? What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 17th Tactical Group existed. Its command was in the village of Pelagicevo. It was within the 17th Tuzla Corps, whose commander was General Savo Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now: Who was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 17th Tactical Group was Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the command was in the village of Pelagicevo. Can you say how far away from Bosanski Samac this village is and in which municipality the village is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The village of Pelagicevo is one of the biggest villages in Posavina, I think. In territorial terms, it then belonged to the municipality of Gradacac. It is about 40 kilometres away from Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army was part of the municipality of Brcko, part of the municipality of Gradacac, Samac, and part of the municipality of Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please - and I'm not objecting, I'm merely asking perhaps a question of the Defence - Mr. Pisarevic led this witness to two meetings that took place in late 1991, at which this particular witness attended and which was addressed by army officers. The significance of that evidence is not apparent to me, other than the fact that the meetings occurred and this witness went there. It's got to be relevant to the proceedings in this case in some way, and apparently relevant. On the face of it, the evidence doesn't mean anything. If it's related to the birth of the 4th Detachment, then that should be made clear. If it's related to some other issue, then it should be made clear. Otherwise you will be left with evidence of this witness went to two meetings. So what? What happened? What was the point of that evidence? And I submit that we need to clarify that for you to make head or tail of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. I'm so sorry, but my learned friend should have been just a bit more patient. We would have come to the 4th Detachment and these meetings. Just a bit more patience, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I feared that, and in that case, I apologise, and Mr. Pisarevic will develop his evidence in the way he sees fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said what the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group was, and you said the municipality of Samac. Please, since the municipality of Samac is quite special, there is part of the municipality that is on the other side of the Bosna River, was part of the municipality, was that part of the municipality that is on the other side of the Bosna River also within the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: On the left bank of the Bosna River is the area of the municipality of Odzak, which was not part of the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The village of Prud, it was within the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Did it enter the zone of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The village of Prud seceded from the municipality of Bosanski Samac. As far as I know, in it there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll go to -- move on to that later. Just tell me: What was the answer?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we've come to the second meeting. What was said by Commander Nikolic at these meetings? What kind of decisions were adopted in relation to the organisation of the 17th Tactical Group and the objectives of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The objectives of the Yugoslav People's Army in this area were to protect the population, to safeguard certain facilities, the territory, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Commander Nikolic then call upon the reserve officers to join the Yugoslav People's Army, irrespective of their ethnic, religious, or other affiliations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The motto of these meetings was that all reserve officers should join the Yugoslav People's Army, so that the entire population in this territory could be kept safe through a concerted effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What followed after these meetings? What kind of decision was made by the commander of the 17th Tactical Group regarding the establishment of detachments?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: After these meetings were held, and of course, an analysis was made of the events that could have followed, on the 5th of January, 1992, the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, passed an order on the establishment of the 4th Detachment in the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army was solely the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the 17th Tactical Group, were there any other detachments that were established in the territory of the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 4th Detachment was only one of the detachments within the 17th Tactical Group. There was the 1st Detachment, the 2nd Detachment, the 3rd Detachment, and the 5th Detachment as well. I mean in addition to the 4th one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, including the 4th Detachment. On that occasion, when the 4th Detachment was established, the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, who was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, did he also establish the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The order on the establishment of the 4th Detachment also set out its area of responsibility, but, at the same time, the command of the 4th Detachment was established too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who was appointed commander of the 4th Detachment in this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I, Radovan Antic, was appointed commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was appointed deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Captain Jovo Savic was appointed deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other positions in the detachment command, like assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Any command, within its command, in addition to the commander and the deputy commander, has a number of assistant commanders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who were the assistant commanders in your detachment, and what posts did they hold?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: My assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs was Simo Zaric, Sergeant Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who were the other assistant commanders you had?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: I had an assistant commander for logistics, Mr. Miroslav Tadic. Then we had an operations officer. That was Mehmed Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now: What was the organisational structure of the 4th Detachment? What kind of organisational units were included in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Every unit of the Yugoslav People's Army has a prescribed establishment. According to this establishment, the 4th Detachment consisted of four companies, and within each company there were squads, or rather, platoons and squads. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We saw that the command was set up by the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. Who appointed the commanding officers of the companies, squads, and platoons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The commanding officers of companies were established by the commander of the detachment, and the commanding officers of platoons and squads, respectively, were proposed by the company commander and were actually appointed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What was the ethnic make-up of the members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was of a mixed ethnic make-up, or rather, it had members from the ranks of all three peoples, and there were even members of some national minorities who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this the case also in the command staff? I mean the command companies, the command squads?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is this mixed composition of the superior staff at the 4th Detachment. That was also fully respected. So at the command we also had an officer who was Muslim, we had two commanders of companies who were Muslims; then we had squad commander, or commanders, who were also from the Muslim -- with a Muslim ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now discuss the way the 17th Tactical Group operated, and of course the 4th Detachment. Who were you subordinated to, specifically, within the 17th Tactical Group? Whose orders did you have to comply with?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: All detachment commanders were subordinate exclusively to the commander of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And your deputy detachment commander and your assistants and the commanders of squads, who were they subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: At the command of the detachment, all members were subordinate to the commander of that detachment. But in case that he was absent, the authority would be taken over by his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You, as a detachment commander, would you be able to place the detachment into any kind of operation without first receiving the order of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: None of the detachments could autonomously undertake any operation without receiving the appropriate order of their superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Within the 4th Detachment, any executive order, could it have been given by anyone amongst your deputies or assistants, if you were present there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: None of the executive orders, without the knowledge of the commander, none of the members of the command could have issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, now could you please explain: What was the role of the assistant commander for intelligence and security matters and for morale? That is, what was Simo Zaric's authority and what were your methods of work, and his tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The task of the assistant commander for intelligence and security matters, this was to gather the relevant security information in relation to the members of the 4th Detachment, and all other events that could be relevant or important for the members of the 4th Detachment, and of course the processing of data, and also, along the chain of command, the assistant could undertake certain activities. That is, he had to report to the commander and to his superior, according to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, let us clarify the chain of command, and can you tell us about this responsibility, that is, the obligation, of Mr. Zaric, that is, the assistant commander for security matters, in the detachment where he is per establishment and also in relation to the higher organs of security and intelligence matters that existed as part of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Assistant for security and intelligence matters was an autonomous organ within the detachment, in the stage of gathering the security information. And then he had the obligation, according to the chain of command, that is, according to the vertical of the chain of command, along the vertical line, he had to report to his superior officer, to the assistant commander of the 17th Tactical Group, who is in charge of security and intelligence matters. That is the main rule in the Yugoslav People's Army. That is the principle of superiority and subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if you recall: Who was this officer, this security officer? That is, who was the chief of the security and intelligence department at the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: In the 17th Tactical Group, the chief for security and intelligence matters was Maksim Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, apart from these tasks that he carried out in security and intelligence, did you task Simo Zaric to conduct any other work that he had to do in the interest of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Zaric was my assistant for security and intelligence matters, in terms of establishment structure, this is what he had to do: He was in charge of morale of the unit and for information, either in terms of internal information or external information, in relation to other subjects, that is, the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, was he able to do anything without acquiring, prior to that, an order or an authority to do anything whatsoever, any tasks that he did?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for the aforementioned matters, he always had the obligation to inform his commander about his planned activities that he would undertake in the period to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, Mr. Zaric, was he able to go to an official meeting for the 4th Detachment without you authorising him to go there and represent the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you issue such orders and authority to Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have issued such authority to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, a matter that you might find, and again, I hope I'm not preempting Mr. Pisarevic here. He may be coming to this issue. But it seems to me that it might have been bypassed and I'm concerned about it, is the witness saying that as far as the chain of command was concerned, Mr. Zaric reported directly to Simeunovic in the 17th Tactical Group, bypassing this witness, or whether the reporting to the command in the 17th Tactical Group went via this witness, through this witness. From the way the evidence came out, that wasn't clear, and it's important, I submit, for you to know that, whether, in the course of reporting on intelligence issues, Mr. Zaric went not only to the 17th Tactical Group but through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Some of these things you clarify in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness has answered. But never mind. We won't go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: When, or rather, where was located the command of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The accommodation facility of the command of the 4th Detachment was allocated by the decision of the secretariat for National Defence, and it was located in the Sit company building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How much of the premises did you have in that building?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: We had one office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In that building where you had one office, did you have put up any kind of symbol, any kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since we were the regular unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, on the building of our command, at a prominent place, facing the main thoroughfare, we had the flag flying of the SFRY and of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you're an officer, can you tell me: What regulations were applied in the operating procedures of the Yugoslav People's Army in the 17th Tactical Group, and in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment operated in accordance to all legal regulations that were in force then, which were the law on National Defence, the law on the armed forces, the law on the military service, then the relevant instructions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now speak a little about this 4th Detachment. The 4th Detachment, did it have any exercises, manoeuvres, and how did it operate?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: From the time when it was established, that is, from the order of the 5th of January, when it was established, members of the 4th Detachment had the relevant exercises, that is, training, mostly in shooting, training in shooting, then training in handling infantry weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where was this training conducted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: These training sessions were conducted on the training ground of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Specifically, this was the training ground in Potocari, in the municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us: What was the weapons -- what were the weapons that the members of the 4th Detachment had?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment had only infantry weapons, and by that I mean automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifle, and automatic and semi-automatic machine-gun, and a hand-held rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us: How were the weapons issued to the members of the 4th Detachment, the weapons that you have just mentioned now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment did not have its warehouse. It had no storage places, and the quartermaster's equipment and the weapons this 4th Detachment had issued directly from the warehouse and the storage spaces of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to now ask the usher if he could show a document, and that we would like to tender as evidence. This is precisely the permits to bear weapons, which is exactly how we demonstrate how the 4th Detachment members were authorised to have weapons issued to them. And could we have one copy for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you have a look at the document, please. Did you have a look at this document? Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now just could you please put it on the ELMO, and the usher will help you, so that the other people in the courtroom can see it, especially the accused. Thank you. Were you in a position to see this before, and can you tell us what does this document mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: This document is a permit, a weapons permit, and it was issued by the 17th Tactical Group. And on this permit, certificate permit, there would be the type of the weapon that is entered, that is issued to the named member, and his obligation was to carry this permit on his person. And here, as I can see, the signature is that of the Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read in the top-left corner what it says.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "Military post code TG 17." And then there are some numbers: 943/1/9. And then it says the date, being the 21st [as interpreted] of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't need to read any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we have a number? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, maybe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One small correction for the transcript. Here on page 89, line 7. It says: "Between the 21st of March, 1992." And what I heard witness actually stated was the 1st of March, 1992. So maybe this can be clarified with the witness. I believe that it is obvious from the document, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- let's have the number first so we can --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D48/4 and D48/4 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This was just a small correction in the transcript. The date that you read from this document a minute ago, was it the 1st of March or --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC
